lead: A pattern is the mould-maker's copy of the casting. It is packed in sand, withdrawn, and the space left behind is filled with liquid metal. The metal shrinks as it cools, and the pattern must be pulled out of the sand, so the pattern is never exactly the size of the finished part. Allowances fix that difference. Patterns decide the mould cavity, the parting line and much of the tooling cost, so a 1% error in a pattern makes every casting in the batch 1% wrong.
prereq: You need: 1.1 Sand casting and moulding sand properties, because a pattern is only meaningful as the shape that is packed in sand.

sections.h3: The pattern is a copy, not the part

blocks.text: A pattern is the positive replica of the casting. Ram sand around it, withdraw it, and the empty cavity left behind is the negative that the metal fills. A core box does the same job for a core.

Three objects are easy to confuse. The part is the finished machined component on the drawing. The casting is the rough metal that leaves the mould, with machining stock still on it. The pattern is the tool that makes the mould for that casting.

The pattern is not the same size as the casting for two reasons. Liquid metal shrinks when it freezes and cools (see 1.5), so the cavity must be bigger than the cold casting. And the pattern must come out of the rammed sand without tearing the cavity walls, so vertical faces are tapered and the pattern may be rapped before withdrawal. Each effect becomes an allowance.
A pattern is reused many times, so its material is chosen by how many moulds it must survive and how fine a surface the casting needs.
The shape of the casting and the batch size decide the pattern type.

items: Solid pattern: one piece with no joint. Cheapest, used when a flat face can act as the parting line.
Split pattern: two halves meeting at the parting line, located by dowel pins. Used when the shape cannot be withdrawn from one side.
Cope-and-drag pattern: also two halves, but each half is moulded separately in the cope and the drag and is located by pins in the flask. Used for large castings.

Match plate pattern: the cope half and the drag half mounted on opposite faces of one plate, with runners and gates attached. One ramming makes both halves, so it suits machine moulding and long runs.
Sweep pattern: a profile board rotated about a vertical or horizontal axis over a bed of sand. Used for large circular shapes such as a bell or a big flange, where a full pattern would be huge.
Skeleton pattern: a frame carrying only the outline; the sand inside is strickled to shape by hand. Used for very large, simple shapes such as a big rectangular box.
Loose piece pattern: the main body plus separate pieces at projections that would block withdrawal; the loose pieces are drawn out after the main pattern.

blocks.text: An allowance is a deliberate difference between the pattern and the casting. Four allowances make the pattern bigger or differently shaped; one makes it smaller. Apply them in a fixed order and state the order, because the examiner marks it.

blocks.where: L_pattern is the pattern length in mm along one direction; L_casting is the casting length in mm in the same direction; s is the shrinkage as a decimal fraction (10 mm/m = 0.01); m is the machining allowance in mm on that dimension, zero if the surface is not machined.

items: Shrinkage allowance: positive. The cavity must be larger than the cold casting. Values depend on the metal; handbooks quote about 10 mm/m (1%) for grey cast iron, about 20 mm/m (2%) for steel and about 13 to 16 mm/m for aluminium alloys. Treat these as examples, not constants — use the figure your foundry has proved for its metal and mould.
Machining allowance: positive stock on surfaces that will be machined, so the tool can reach clean metal. It grows with casting size and with the roughness of the process.
Draft allowance: taper on vertical faces, the faces parallel to the direction of withdrawal. Without it the sand tears. It is quoted in degrees, commonly 0.5° to 2°, and is larger on internal faces.
Distortion allowance: long, thin, U- or V-shaped castings warp as they cool; the pattern is given the opposite camber so the casting straightens out.

Shake (rapping) allowance: negative. Rapping the pattern before withdrawal enlarges the cavity, so the pattern is made a little smaller. It is a fraction of a millimetre and is often neglected in sums that say so.

blocks.text: No single material wins everywhere. Wood is easy to shape and cheap but moves with moisture. Metal holds size and gives a better surface but is heavy and costly. Plastic sits between the two.

figure.caption: The pattern length is built from the part length by adding each allowance in turn. In this example only the shrinkage of 8 mm is added, so an 800 mm part needs an 808 mm pattern.

spec.title: From part drawing to pattern size
spec.aria: A vertical flow chart showing an 800 mm part drawing gaining an 8 mm shrinkage allowance and then moving through machining and draft allowances to a final 808 mm pattern length.

examples.question: A grey cast iron block is to be 800 mm long after casting and cleaning. The foundry uses a shrinkage allowance of 10 mm/m for grey cast iron. The 800 mm dimension is not machined, draft is applied on the sides only, shake is neglected and distortion is nil. Find the shrinkage allowance and the pattern length.
steps: Convert the shrinkage to a fraction: s = 10 mm/m = 10 ÷ 1000 = 0.01 mm per mm, which is 1%.
Shrinkage allowance = L_casting × s = 800 mm × 0.01 = 8 mm.
Machining allowance on this dimension m = 0 mm, because the surface is not machined.
Pattern length = L_casting × (1 + s) + m = 800 × 1.01 + 0 = 808 mm.
Check in reverse: when the 808 mm cavity fills and the metal cools, it contracts by about 1%, giving 808 × 0.99 = 799.9 mm, which is the required 800 mm to within a tenth of a millimetre.
examples.answer: The shrinkage allowance is 8 mm and the pattern length is 808 mm.
examples.check:
L_casting = 800.0          # mm
s = 10.0 / 1000.0           # mm per mm
m = 0.0                     # mm, surface not machined
allowance = L_casting * s
L_pattern = L_casting * (1 + s) + m
print(allowance)
print(L_pattern)
print(L_pattern * (1 - s))

traps: 10 mm/m is 1%, not 10%: an 800 mm casting grows by 8 mm, not 80 mm.
Draft goes on vertical faces — the faces parallel to withdrawal — never on the parting plane.
Shake allowance is negative; the pattern is made smaller, not larger.

A match plate is a mounting method, not a material. A split pattern and a cope-and-drag pattern are both two-piece, but the cope-and-drag halves are located by pins in the flask, not by dowels in the pattern.
Shrinkage is a linear allowance applied once to each dimension; it is not a volume percentage, so do not cube it.

quiz.q: Define a pattern and state why it is not the same size as the casting.
quiz.a: A pattern is the replica of the casting used to make the mould cavity. It differs in size because liquid metal shrinks on cooling, and because the pattern must be withdrawn from the sand (draft, shake).

quiz.q: Why is the shake allowance negative?
quiz.a: Rapping the pattern before withdrawal enlarges the mould cavity, so the pattern is made smaller so that the enlarged cavity gives the correct casting size.

quiz.q: Why is a match plate pattern preferred for machine moulding?
quiz.a: Both halves sit on one plate with the gating attached, so one ramming of the flask produces the cope and the drag, the halves cannot go out of alignment, and the plate can be bolted to the machine table and reused without resetting.

quiz.q: A part 500 mm long is cast with a shrinkage allowance of 12 mm/m. Both ends need 3 mm of machining stock. Use L_pattern = L_casting × (1 + s) + m and find the pattern length.
quiz.a: s = 12 mm/m = 0.012; total machining stock m = 3 + 3 = 6 mm. L_pattern = 500 × 1.012 + 6 = 506 + 6 = 512 mm.

quiz.q: Which pattern would you choose for a bell of 1.5 m diameter, and why?
quiz.a: A sweep pattern. A profile board rotated about a vertical axis sweeps the circular cavity out of a small amount of pattern material; a full solid pattern of that size would be heavy, costly and hard to store.

quiz.q: A pattern is withdrawn without draft by knocking it with a mallet. Predict the defects in the casting.
quiz.a: The sand tears on the vertical faces, giving rough patches and sand inclusions; knocking breaks the cavity edges, so the casting has ragged corners and the mould needs repair; the enlarged cavity also makes the casting oversize. Remedy: add draft and rap gently.

quiz.q: A 1 m long thin cast iron bar arrives bowed after cooling. Which allowance was missing and how is it applied?
quiz.a: The distortion (camber) allowance. The pattern is given an equal and opposite curvature, so the bar warps back to straight as it cools; the amount is found from the shop's past castings or from simulation, not from a universal constant.

beyond: Not for the exam. Foundries now print moulds and patterns directly in sand by binder jetting from the CAD model, so no physical pattern is stored for short runs (see Unit 7). Shrinkage is checked by casting simulation before the first pour, and allowances are entered as scale factors in the CAM model. The same allowance logic appears in polymer moulding, where moulds are cut oversize for shrinkage. Search for pattern allowance standards, patternless moulding and casting simulation.
